newsitem.title: JAPAN: Analysts say Japan should reexamine aid budget.
newsitem.headline: Analysts say Japan should reexamine aid budget.

text.p: The Peru hostage crisis could force Japan to rethink what one analyst on Friday described as "faceless chequebook diplomacy" that did not take enough account of where aid money went.
As the world's largest aid donor, Japan in 1995 disbursed $14.73 billion to developing countries through its Official Development Assistance (ODA) agency.

This week's takeover of the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima by guerrillas, who said they chose Japan as a target "due to the constant meddling of the Japanese government in Peru", has turned a spotlight on the aid issue.
Japan started giving massive economic aid to Peru when President Alberto Fujimori, the son of Japanese immigrants, became head of the nation.
Peru, home to some 80,000 people of Japanese ancestry, is the biggest recipient of Japanese economic aid in Latin America, receiving a total of 200 billion yen ($1.75 billion) up until 1995.
When Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto visited Lima last August, he pledged 62.8 billion yen ($550 million) in fresh low-interest development loans to Peru.
Critics said the hostage drama in Lima could set the stage for Japan to re-examine its policy of assistance of simply opening its cheque book and disbursing funds.
Japan should should shift the focus from quantity to quality to win the gratitude of recipient countries, said Hideaki Kase, an international diplomacy analyst.
"The Japanese government and people think it is better to give money rather than bleeding themselves," Kase told Reuters.
"Japan, which looks like a lazy fat pig, must stop its faceless checkbook diplomacy. You can't buy the hearts of people with money," he said.

Atsuyuki Sassa, a former top bureaucreat in the prime minister's office, said the time might have come to re-examine conditions on Japanese aid, particularly stipulations that it should be money, be government-to-government and not interfere in a recipient's internal affairs.
"In the case of underdeveloped nations, particularly totalitarian ones, sometimes our aid goes the wrong way and into the wrong people's pocket," Sasse told Reuters.
He suggested more aid should be in the form of food, non-governmental agencies like the Red Cross should get help, and Japan should not be so wary of complaining if it felt aid was being abused.
"Maybe we should interfere if there is abuse of our aid by it going on military construction or trickling away through corruption," he said.

"Japan should have second thoughts if the general public in Peru believes both that Japan unconditionally supports the strong-arm attitude of the president (Fujimori) and that Japan's economic assistance benefits only a particular segment of the population," The Asahi Shimbun said in an editorial on Friday. ($1=114 yen)
